context: Al-Adiyat is Makkan in the reckoning of the majority, from the years when the Quran was training its first listeners with images their world already loved. Nothing stirred an Arab audience like horses, and the surah opens with a cavalry raid in five strokes of sound: mares panting, hooves striking sparks in the dark, the charge at dawn, the trail of dust, the plunge into the middle of the enemy. Then the oath lands its verdict somewhere no one expected: not on the enemy, but on man himself.

The word chosen is kanud, deeply ungrateful, and the classical commentators unpack it as the one who counts misfortunes and forgets gifts. In a city of traders the next line cut deeper: his love of wealth is shadid, intense, violent. The early community heard the contrast the surah paints without stating: the horse spends itself utterly for a master who only feeds it, while man withholds himself from the Master who gave him everything, and the surah walks that ingratitude forward to the morning the graves are poured out.
name_story: The surah is named for al-adiyat, the charging steeds of its first oath, the raiding mares heard panting before they are seen. Early sources cite it by this first word, and no other name is soundly attached. Even its name gallops.

movements.note: Five oath-verses paint the raid in pure sound and motion, panting breath, struck sparks, dawn charge, stirred dust, the plunge into the midst, loyalty and fury spent for a human master.
Against the horse’s spent devotion stands the rider: deeply ungrateful to his Lord, himself a witness to it, and fierce in his love of wealth.
The cure for ingratitude is one question: does he not know that when what is in the graves is poured out and what is in the chests is gathered, their Lord that Day is fully aware of them.

themes.t: The loyal beast, the disloyal man
themes.d: The horse gives everything for oats and a stable; man hoards himself against the Lord who made him. The surah lets an animal shame its rider.
The heart that tallies every hardship and files every blessing under deserved: the surah names the accounting error at the root of unbelief.
Love of good things is not condemned as feeling but exposed as fever, shadid, strong enough to shape a whole life’s direction.
The surah ends not at opened graves but at opened hearts: hussila ma fis-sudur, the harvest of what chests hid, the deeper of the two exhumations.

heart: Read slowly, Al-Adiyat starts in the ears and ends in the conscience. The opening verses are onomatopoeia you can feel, dabhan, qadhan, breath and sparks, and then the surah reins the whole cavalry to a halt in front of a mirror. Inna al-insana li-rabbihi la-kanud: the reader is invited to check his own ledger and finds, honestly, that he remembers his losses in detail and his gifts in general. That is kanud, and recognizing it in oneself is the surah doing its work.

The last movement quietly relocates the Day of Judgment. We imagine it as the emptying of graves, and the surah grants that, then goes further inward: the gathering of what the chests contained. Motives, grudges, hidden loves, the reasons under the deeds. The reciter who understands verse ten begins that same night to clean not just his record but his interior, because both are scheduled for daylight.

passages.why: The oath’s landing point: the verdict of ingratitude, worth hearing with your own accounts in mind.
One verse holds the fever of wealth-love up to the light: is its grip this strong on me.
The deeper resurrection: not the graves but the chests, when what hearts concealed is gathered out.

connections.why: Az-Zalzalah gives the same Day its scales: the chests unsealed here are weighed there, atom by atom.
At-Takathur follows the same fierce wealth-love to its terminus, the visit to the graves this surah sees poured out.

virtue.text: No authentic hadith assigns a specific reward to reciting Al-Adiyat, and it needs no certificate: its virtue is the honesty of its mirror, an oath of Allah over the state of the human heart before its Lord.
